title: Explain any three microservices design patterns in detail (e.g. API Gateway, Circuit Breaker, Database-per-Service).
shortTitle: Three microservices design patterns in detail

s1_definition.profdef: Three foundational microservices patterns are the API Gateway, the Circuit Breaker, and Database-per-Service. The API Gateway is a single entry point that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, and request aggregation so clients never talk to services directly. The Circuit Breaker wraps a remote call and tracks its failure rate, moving from CLOSED to OPEN to fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy, then HALF_OPEN to test recovery, which stops failures from cascading. Database-per-Service gives each service exclusive ownership of its data store, so services are decoupled at the data layer and can evolve their schema independently.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the API Gateway is the reception desk that checks your ID, limits how many people enter per minute, and points you to the right department. The Circuit Breaker is the "counter temporarily closed" sign: when the cash desk cannot serve, staff put up the sign so customers do not keep queuing and jamming the lobby. Database-per-Service is giving each department its own private ledger that no other department can open directly; if the loan department wants account data, it must ask the account department, not peek into its books.
s1_definition.oneliner: API Gateway is the single front door, Circuit Breaker fails fast to stop cascades, and Database-per-Service keeps each service's data private so services stay independent.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Three foundational microservices patterns are the API Gateway, the Circuit Breaker, and Database-per-Service. The API Gateway is a single entry point that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, and request aggregation so clients never talk to services directly. The Circuit Breaker wraps a remote call and tracks its failure rate, moving from CLOSED to OPEN to fail fast when a dependency is unhealthy, then HALF_OPEN to test recovery, which stops failures from cascading. Database-per-Service gives each service exclusive ownership of its data store, so services are decoupled at the data layer and can evolve their schema independently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, the API Gateway is the reception desk that checks your ID, limits how many people enter per minute, and points you to the right department. The Circuit Breaker is the "counter temporarily closed" sign: when the cash desk cannot serve, staff put up the sign so customers do not keep queuing and jamming the lobby. Database-per-Service is giving each department its own private ledger that no other department can open directly; if the loan department wants account data, it must ask the account department, not peek into its books.

**One line to remember:** API Gateway is the single front door, Circuit Breaker fails fast to stop cascades, and Database-per-Service keeps each service's data private so services stay independent.

sections.s2_technical:
The API Gateway pattern centralizes everything a client should not repeat. A route is a predicate plus filters: in Spring Cloud Gateway you route `Path=/api/v1/payments/**` to `lb://payment-service` and attach filters such as a JWT auth filter and a `RequestRateLimiter`. The gateway can also aggregate: one client call to `/api/v1/dashboard` fans out to the account, payment, and card services and merges the responses, saving the mobile app three round trips. Crucially the gateway hides the internal topology, so you can split or rename a service without changing clients.

The Circuit Breaker pattern protects callers from a failing dependency. With Resilience4j you annotate `@CircuitBreaker(name="accountService", fallbackMethod="debitFallback")`. The breaker counts outcomes over a sliding window; when the failure rate crosses the threshold it flips to OPEN and every call fails instantly by invoking the fallback, for example returning a queued-for-retry response. After a wait it moves to HALF_OPEN and lets a few trial calls through; if they succeed it closes, otherwise it reopens. You always pair it with a timeout so a slow call counts as a failure, and often a bulkhead so the dependency cannot consume all threads.

Database-per-Service means the Payment Service owns the payments tables and the Account Service owns the accounts tables, with no shared schema and no cross-service joins. If the Payment Service needs the holder's name it either calls the Account Service synchronously or keeps a local read-model copy kept fresh by consuming `account-events` from Kafka. This gives independence: the Account team can change its schema freely because no other service reads its tables directly. The cost is that you lose cross-service ACID transactions and must use the Saga pattern and eventual consistency. The senior-level nuance is that these three patterns reinforce each other: Database-per-Service forces network calls, network calls need circuit breakers, and the gateway is where you enforce auth and rate limits for all of them in one place.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the mobile app loads Rajesh's dashboard. Problem 1 — without a gateway the app would call three services directly, embedding internal addresses and repeating auth in each call. This is exactly what the API Gateway solves: one authenticated call that fans out and aggregates. Problem 2 — the Account Service goes slow during a deploy, and the Payment Service keeps calling it until all its threads are stuck. This is exactly what the Circuit Breaker solves by failing fast with a fallback. Problem 3 — the Payment Service wants the account holder's name, and a junior engineer is tempted to query the accounts table directly. This is exactly what Database-per-Service forbids: the Payment Service must call the Account Service or use its own read model.

The mini-project builds a `ApiGateway` that authenticates and aggregates, a `CircuitBreaker` that trips after repeated failures and serves a fallback, and an `AccountServiceClient` plus `PaymentService` that each own their data and communicate only through calls. A runnable demo loads the dashboard, then forces the Account Service to fail and shows the breaker opening and the fallback kicking in.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a dashboard request for Rajesh (SAV2001) with a valid JWT, then the Account Service goes down.

Step 1: The request hits the API Gateway. The gateway checks the JWT. If missing it rejects with a security error; here the token is valid so the request proceeds, and the gateway is the only place auth is enforced.

Step 2: The gateway aggregates by calling the Payment Service's `resolveHolder`. The Payment Service does not own the holder name, so it must call the Account Service rather than read its table.

Step 3: The Payment Service wraps the call in the circuit breaker. The breaker is CLOSED, so the real call runs and returns "Rajesh Kumar". The gateway merges this into the dashboard response.

Step 4: Now the Account Service goes down. The first failing call increments the failure count to 1 and serves the fallback "NAME_UNAVAILABLE". The second failing call reaches the threshold of 2 and flips the breaker to OPEN.

Step 5: On the third attempt the breaker is OPEN, so it fails fast without even calling the Account Service and immediately serves the fallback, moving to HALF_OPEN to test recovery on the next real attempt. The system stays responsive even though a dependency is down.

```text
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO === Healthy: gateway auth + aggregate ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO Gateway authenticated request for SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO REMOTE lookup holder for SAV2001
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO Response: {accountId=SAV2001, holder=Rajesh Kumar}
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO === Account Service down: breaker trips ===
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 SEVERE Call failed (1/2): Account Service unavailable
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO Attempt 1 → {accountId=SAV2001, holder=NAME_UNAVAILABLE (fallback)} [breaker=CLOSED]
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 SEVERE Call failed (2/2): Account Service unavailable
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO Attempt 2 → {accountId=SAV2001, holder=NAME_UNAVAILABLE (fallback)} [breaker=OPEN]
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 WARNING Breaker OPEN — fail fast, serving fallback
Oct 24, 2026 11:52:30 INFO Attempt 3 → {accountId=SAV2001, holder=NAME_UNAVAILABLE (fallback)} [breaker=HALF_OPEN]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Client: GET /api/v1/dashboard?accountId=SAV2001  (JWT)
    │
    ▼
  API Gateway  (Pattern 1)
    │ verify JWT  → authenticate once
    │ aggregate ───→ PaymentService.resolveHolder("SAV2001")
    ▼
  PaymentService (owns payments DB only — Pattern 3)
    │ needs holder name → must CALL Account Service
    ▼
  CircuitBreaker  (Pattern 2)
    │
    ├─ CLOSED → real call → AccountServiceClient.holderName() → "Rajesh Kumar"
    │
    ├─ after 2 failures → OPEN → fail fast → "NAME_UNAVAILABLE"
    │
    └─ HALF_OPEN → next call is a trial
    ▼
  Gateway merges → {accountId, holder}
    ▼
  Response to client
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
When asked to explain microservices patterns in detail, I pick the three that nearly every real system needs and show how they reinforce each other. The first is the API Gateway. It is the single entry point that handles routing, authentication, rate limiting, and request aggregation, so clients never talk to services directly. In my banking work at National Bank of India, the mobile app makes one authenticated call to the gateway for Rajesh's dashboard, and the gateway fans out to the account and payment services and merges the responses, which hides the internal topology and lets us split or rename services without touching clients.

The second is the Circuit Breaker. It wraps a remote call and tracks the failure rate over a sliding window. When failures cross the threshold it flips from closed to open and every call fails instantly by invoking a fallback, so the caller stays responsive instead of piling up threads waiting on a dead dependency. After a wait it moves to half-open and lets a few trial calls through to test recovery. I always pair it with a timeout, so a slow call counts as a failure, and often a bulkhead.

The third is Database-per-Service. Each service exclusively owns its data store, so the Payment Service owns the payments tables and the Account Service owns the accounts tables, with no shared schema and no cross-service joins. When the Payment Service needs the account holder's name, it calls the Account Service or keeps a local read model updated from events; it never queries the other service's tables.

The reason I choose these three together is that they interlock. Database-per-Service forces services to talk over the network, those network calls are exactly what the Circuit Breaker protects, and the API Gateway is the one place where I enforce authentication and rate limiting for all of them. The tradeoff I am always honest about is that Database-per-Service costs us cross-service ACID transactions, which is why we adopt the Saga pattern and accept eventual consistency.
